replies.author: @Ariale618
replies.text:
@Terror_OfficialGlad that we can have a proper discussion!

When you said that Affricates were a third separation (of course worded differently), I was mainly challenging this view because I thought that you were saying that Affricates were essentially an equal classification to Pulmonic and Non-Pulmonic consonants. Now that I know this is not the case, I won't challenge you any further on this.

On 'dialectal allophones', you probably shouldn't include these in your counting. Because almost every native English dialect (all that I know of) do not differentiate between more than one rhotic (even the alveolar tap is not considered rhotic by American or Australian speakers, among others) I am challenging you on why you are including allophones. If you include these rhotics without listing them as allophones, then why wouldn't other allophones, e.g. /ħ/ for /h/ be counted? and that is excluding the rarer allophones of course. When you transcribe languages, I would recommend that you only include phonemes; the sounds which make up the base of the language, not sounds which only appear in certain positions and do not contrast with other sounds (specifically those which you are trying to separate the sound from) in the same position. For example, the dental fricatives /θ, ð/ form minimal pairs despite historically having been one sound. For example, 'sheath' (IPA: /ʃiːθ/) forms a minimal pair with 'sheathe' (IPA: /ʃiːð/). You need at least one minimal pair to distinguish fully phonemic sounds from allophones, but preferably more to prove that the sound is fully phonemic and not just a singular case or an unchanged loanword. This is just one example, there are several.

And thank you for clearing it up, that you were talking about Proto-Northwest Caucasian, not Proto-Circassian (or Proto-Kirkassian) as you were saying.

I had gotten the impression from your previous comments that you were arguing that /kʷ/ was an independent phoneme. For example, you listed Proto-Germanic 'kwikwaz' (or kwíkwâz) and used it to justify your position. If this isn't the case then we both agree yet again.

From what you are saying, it sounds like you've taken every sound (including allophonic) from modern NC languages, and have used them to prove a huge consonant inventory for the proto language under your reasoning. I might be wrong, but I haven't actually seen your reconstruction in full. Maybe an example would help? I was just pointing out that the number seemed to be extremelt inflated and is probably not very close to the actual number, since 180 to 181 consonant sounds for a proto language sounds incorrect.

And if you want to learn more about Russian, I promise you it's very interesting. I've learned a fair bit myself. You mention that you have family who speak it; what's your native language? Just because I'm interested

I got the idea that you stated that 'million' has a lateral fricative because earlier, in one of your previous comments, you stated that 'the secondary l in this cluster completely changes the consonant to a lateral fricative'. If this isn't what you meant, then maybe you should've worded it more carefully. If you meant a palatal lateral approximant, like you are saying now, then that's fine. I think I got confused with your older comment because I scrolled back too far!

Just a note though... Not very many Welsh speakers use /ɬ/, and it is usually allophonic (when excluding extremely archaic border dialects), because Welsh also has /l/ as a contrastive phoneme. It is important to specify that just because a language has a sound does not make it a phonemic sound, so allophones always have to be accounted for. I know I bring this up a lot, but it is crucial to distinguish allophones from phonemic sounds, otherwise a reader of your work might mistake your words to mean something completely different, regardless if you mean the opposite.

Interesting that you keep using a modified latin script with diacritics to transcribe certain words. Is this just something that you like to do or is it more of a hobby with conlanging or designing a script?

And again, I respect your usage of 'Kirkassian'. I was saying that it might take too much effort to explain to every reader. Before, though, it was rude of me to say that it isn't the correct pronunciation, but hopefully you can understand why it can be confusing to use your own terms. I also do this though! When I talk about foreign place names, I sometimes use the endonym. I've gotten a lot of weird looks for pronouncing placenames differently to the anglicised form, like 'Łódź' in Poland!

My point about the huge consonant inventory in your reconstruction of PNC was simply that the number seems too high, and that many of the sounds would indeed be indistinguishable as you note, which is why I am challenging such a high count. Remember that sounds change constantly, and that what you reconstruct might not reflect the original sound. Then again, I haven't made my own PNC reconstruction, so my only criticism is that the consonants you listed seem to be too numerous.

I keep on forgetting to use [], instead I keep on using //. This is just me forgetting, usually I make sure to correct myself.

replies.text:

I agree with like 99% of what you're saying, though the part about Affricates I don't feel I need to separate further, as I already separated their formation with diphthongs, ligatures, triphthongs, digraphs and complex graphemes in my counting. Also yes, I am describing each consonant sound from allophones / ăll̈opʰǭnē̂́mătă (such as [a]), and not phonemes / pʰǭnē̂́mătă (such as /a/); it was very intentional.

Starostin, titled A North Caucasian Etymological Dictionary), but my early comments stated ~170 as you did, and yes some would be very rare but so are so many sounds in English (like all of those rhotics). I'm not particularly great at pronouncing alveolar trills for example, but my natural [ʀ] sometimes slips out in words, yet people still recognize it as an /r/ allophone, and therefore its own consonant. I included all English dialectical allophones in my counting because I also did the same with the P-NWC descendant languages. Your details on Russian is interesting, it is merely a side study I've done on it with surface level intuition, as a close member of my family is a linguist who speaks the language.

I also don't know still where you're getting a mention of [ɬ] in anything I was saying, as my million example was about a lateral approximant [ʎ] that does happen in speakers around me. replies.author: @Ariale618
replies.text:
@Terror_OfficialI was pointing out that English does not have any distinctions in secondary articulations. I know that English has 'more consonants' than the average person would believe, I am simply stating that you are classifying certains sounds as being phonemic versus allophonic or dialectal. You cannot inflate a consonant count (like you did with 'million' for example, where you stated that it has a lateral fricative) just because you would like to believe that certain consonants are fully phonemic. I was refuting that, not the idea that English has a good amount of consonants. You yourself stated that English has /kʷ/ as a phoneme, and I was proving to you that you are wrong.

I used ejectives as an example that just because a sound has a superscript marker or regular marker to change the sound does not make it a 'modified' sound off of a base sound. I fully agree with you on this front. I was proving that superscript markers for labialisation, palatalisation, etc. change a consonant into a distinct sound; you were either arguing that they didn't (for Adyghe) or that they do (for English) which was very confusing, so please can you clarify on that front.

Next, you bring up that you 'avoid including labialisation for consonants' because 'they do not generate new IPA keys upon using them with anything but vowels'. You first state that you don't include labialisation for consonants, and then you say that /kʷ/ 'remains the same notation in IPA' and that 'rather than altering the vowel it becomes a secondary articulation'. Now, in the case of Adyghe, labialisation does affect the vowel. The heavy allophony in Adyghe for vowels is dependent on what the previous consonant is. Some vowels, like /ǝ/ as an example, appears as /ɵ~u/ when surrounded by labialised consonants, /ɪ~i/ when surrounded by coronal and palatal consonants, /ɤ/ when surrounded by uvular, pharyngeal and glottal consonants, /ɯ/ when between plain vowels, and the list goes on; consonants evidently alter neighbouring vowels in Adyghe. But this is called allophony, because these vowels cannot occur surrounded by other consonants in the same positions. I am not saying that you said that Adyghe has many vowels; this is an example of why you cannot use allophony to justify an inflated consonant count, and I am using examples which are more likely to be familiar to you, opposed to other languages where I don't know if you have such experience. I can provide examples in English if you really want me to, just say if you do.

If you generally talk about Russian having only '26 consonants', you are being misleading and using flawed counting. You did mention that Russian has 19 consonants which are subject to palatalisation. And... you are wrong again. In terms of sounds which are not disputed, Russian has 15 palatalised consonants. You are yet again mixing up palatal and palatalised consonants. Whilst Russian has 4 palatal consonants, these are not palatalised because they are purely palatal, and that is if you consider /ʑː/ as a phoneme (compared to the fully phonemic /j, t͡ɕ, ɕː). And whether you count /t͡sʲ/, (and controversially) /ɣʲ/ as phonemes, your count of palatal(ised) consonants could range anywhere from 15 to 21. In correct terminology, as they are palatalised and form fully phonemic minimal pairs with the plain variants in modern standard Russian, 15 would be the correct answer. Along with 21 plain, non-palatalised consonants (including palatal), you have ~36 consonants in Russian, not 45. Add the 5 fully phonemic vowels, noting that /ɨ/ is an allophone of /i/ after non-palatalised consonants (with the sole linguistics exception of 'ыкать'), Russian has ~41 sounds. You can try to add allophones, but that is generally not correct methodology, as I have stated, unless you specify that that is including marginal dialectal or liturgical phonemes. 

I stated that Affricates are not their own 'separation' which you said they were. In your own words, here:

"There are 3 basic separations of what classify as consonants. Those are Pulmonic, Non-Pulmonic, and Affricates".

This taxonomical assigment of consonant classification is fundamentally incorrect or at the very best inconsistent. Affricates are a sub-group of consonants as they can co-occur with Pulmonic and Non-Pulmonic. Pulmonic consonants physically cannot co-occur with Non-Pulmonic consonants. Because Affricates can, they do not constitute their own 'separation'. If you really want separations, you can further split Non-Pulmonic into Ejectives (Egressive), Implosives (Ingressive) and Clicks (Ingressive). Whether you consider this valid, I'll leave it up to you, but they fall under the umbrella of Non-Pulmonic, even though they are very different groupings.

Note: You yourself stated 'Proto-Kirkassian from my example, if we included all of their base 2nd articulations, would be around 170 consonants'. You told me that I'm confused when you literally referred to Proto-Circassian?! If you are referring to Proto-Northwest Caucasian, please refer to it as 'PNC' if you are going to use an acronym. That would make it easier for everyone.

Your count of '180~181' consonants is also incorrect, based on modern research. Even Starostin & Nikolayev, the most generous and ludicrous reconstruction, state 167 to 168 consonant phonemes based on whether extremely rare phonemes are included. They only reconstruct two vowels, giving 169 or 170 consonant sounds in total.

However, this is considered very problematic. Recent linguists have debunked this. For example, what S & N reconstruct as *q̇́ʷˤʲ (a pharyngealised, labialised, palatalised, and ejective uvular stop or plosive) is not very likely to say the least. No language has this many contrasting features on a singular consonant, which result in an aerodynamically impossible sound. In many cases of these crazy sounds, linguists have debunked their reconstruction by pointing out that two branches (e.g. Ubykh & Circassian) might have one reconstructed phoneme, whereas another (e.g. Abazgi/Abkhaz-Abaza) has a slightly different sound. They then reconstruct this different sound as existing in PNC, but in reality a vowel change or mutation may have caused the difference, not an inherited consonant that had a unique articulation. Modern reconstructions instead prove that PNC maybe had more vowels, like 4~5, which affected the vowels differently in different branches, and the extreme collapse of vowels in Ubykh and Abazgi in particular led to more secondary articulations arising. Most modern linguists, myself included, treat S & N's reconstruction as having taken consonants from every branch, not bothering to change them, and then resulting in a comically large, hyper-inflated assortment of consonants. I challenge you to pronounce each of the consonants which you listed and maintain a distinction in every single one. If even a single pair of sounds are identical, then you can logically agree that the reconstruction has at the very least concluded in an incorrect consonant.

Note: This is using the highest count of any PNC restruction. If you yourself have found or made a different construction, then this is a different topic entirely. But no documented language has such a high amount of consonant phonemes.

This next segment is not as relevent, as it is about sociolinguistics, not strictly about phonology. I'd still recommend you read it as I'd like to be more mindful moving on.

I respect your decision that English should not split /k/ into multiple phonemes. However, what I do have a problem with is using the term 'Kirkassian'. Although it is nice that you are trying to use a term that closer reflects the native group, it really isn't necessary. The term 'Circassian' is not considered outdated by the vast majority of linguists. Using a different term can confuse people. Bur if you want to use it, that is fine. I didn't know that you were trying to be more respectful, and that's my only problem, that you might want to clarify that on these topics. And 'Circassian' is an umbrella terms for all 12 tribes (with the linguistic exception of 'Ubykh'). Many people who descend from these tribes like the term 'Circassian' because it bridges the gap between them. If that is your choice, fine. I don't mind if you use it, but I personally prefer the internationally accepted version. And you can refer to the wider group as 'Maiotians' or 'Maeotians' but for the sake of being clear, I would use 'Circassian', but it is entirely up to you. I don't want to argue about something like this because it comes down to preference, so I hope we can agree that both of us can use either term. Please just clarify that to other people you are arguing with, to make more sense.

Although I disagree with your arguments, you are a great linguist. Keep on learning, keep on researching, and you will find success. My passion is only because I am very personal about linguistics, but I assure you that I don't mean anything bad towards you as a person.

Secondly, I did not state that ejectives are optional, but that some people don't think of them as separate from their base consonant, which I don't agree with. They are a separate classification under non-Pulmonic.

I'm realizing now, that you believe I'm speaking of Proto-Circassian but I am talking about the Proto-Northwest Caucasian language of the Maiotians. In my original comment I did not state which period I spoke of as "once upon a time", and realize I've confused you into thinking I'm talking about P-C.

Anyways, most of what you're saying I don't believe and you're placing meanings that I don't proclaim. I use the term Kirkassian because the original term used to refer to the people was Kassog, use to refer to the peoples of Zdĭkʰĭ́a/Dzĭkʰĭ́a and the Maotian swamp; with an initial base [k]. I'm perfectly fine with calling them by their endonym of Ādəɣa instead of using Kirkassian, but the secondary term is more recognizable. I for one don't believe English should share both /c/ and /k/ and should instead collapse into /ç/ and /k/. By spelling it with C's, I'd be ignorantly introducing mispronunciation to those that read it.

"Is it [sɚˈsɛɪ.ʒən]?" Serseyʒən
"Is it [kɚˈkɛɪ.ʒən]?" Kerkêyʒən
"Is it [kɚˈt͜ʃɛɪ.ʒən]?" Kerç̌êyʒən
"Is it [sɚˈkɛɪ.ʒən]?" Serkeyʒən
"Is it [t͜ʃɚˈt͜ʃɛɪ.ʒən]?" Ç̌erç̌êyʒən
"Is it [səˈsæ.ʒən]?"  Səsæʒən (Any of these look familiar to you?)

There is no need to confuse a reader. I present [kir.ká.si.an] and the use of this initial [t͡ɕ] sound is a Russian augment. One of the many suspected origins of this word is the awfully Latinized Cercetae. In Greek this was first recorded as Κερκέται (Kerkétai), and as such I spell and say it with [k] rather than giving Circassian an ambiguous pronunciation for readers.

It is possible it's from the Σῐρᾰκοὶ/Σῐρᾰ́κες instead, another of the Maiotians. But in that case we should be calling them Sir(a)keesians, but I don't see anyone using the form [sirˈke.si.an]. This is also through a Turkic inheritance, and I don't see the Ādəɣa running into their arms for anything. Their neighbors, the Ossetians, call them by [sər.gəs].

As to your final line, there is no "Correct" spelling of a poor Romanization (Circassian) of an adaptation (черке́с) of an exonym (Κερκέται/Σῐρᾰ́κες/Shirkess/čērig/چهار/کس/цӕркӕсӕг/K'arš-k') of people that have their own term for themselves. The linguist Lev Lopatinsky who researched the language connected Ādəɣa to Dzĭkʰĭ́a with through an intermediary phase of Adzyge. If they want to take on the Zichian term for their own, then the oldest form would be Ζῐχῐ́της (Zdĭkʰĭ́tē̂s/Dzĭkʰĭ́tē̂s [(zd~d͜z)i.kʰǐ.tɛːs]).

replies.author: @Ariale618
replies.text:
@Terror_OfficialSecondary articulations happen simultaneously with the base consonant, which is why they can be considered to create new consonants, or minimal pairs. You yourself stated that ejectives are optionally included. Yes, they are non-pulmonic, however according to your logic they are not separate sounds because they are all 'versions' of the same sounds but use different airstream mechanisms; you could argue that ejectives are just the same consonant with a ’ as a secondary articulation, which would obviously be incorrect. The IPA provides labialised, pharyngealised, and many other superscript markers to simplify notation, it has nothing to do with how 'valid' the sound is as phonemic, meaning the language contrasts sounds based on whether the lips are rounded or not, for the case of labialised consonants. And for another example, palatalised consonants also contrast. In the Udmurt language, they even created a new letter 'ӥ' to mark when a consonant is NOT palatalised by 'и'. Languages in the caucasus do not generally have such independent letters because it would have to apply to every instance of a palatalised or labialised sound. Instead, in orthography, depending on the language, 'у, в, ә' can be used to mark labialisation. Again, these consonants are simultaneously produced with a secondary articulation. So now you only consider voiced consonants as a 'secondary articulation'? They are at the exact same place of articulation, just with the vibration of the vocal chords. Notice how this is completely wrong? Well just because the IPA doesn't provide independent letters for sounds with secondary articulations does not mean that they cannot formd their own independent phonemes. The entire reason why 'secondary articulation' is a thing is to show simultaneous pronunciation, not just a cluster. As such, co-articulated consonants in the example of Adyghe are absolutely their own phonemes.

You bring up 'palatalised consonants' as having 'their own IPA just for them'. I think that you are confusing palatalISED consonants with PALATAL consonants. Palatal consonants have their own IPA because they are single, plain sounds at the hard palate. Palatalised sounds (which have the secondary articulation 'ʲ') are sounds produced elsewhere, but the tongue is raised towards the hard palate. Irish actually contrasts these, which you should definitely look into. Although contrasting palatal and palatalised consonants is of course very rare, it is not necessary to consider palatalISED consonants independent phonemes instead of clusters. 

Your classification of what is considered a 'separation' of consonants is flawed. You state that there are 'Pulmonic, Non-Pulmonic, and Affricates'. Affricates are actually a manner of articulation, not a separate category; Affricates can be pulmonic or non-pulmonic. Affricates can therefore be considered a sub-type. Co-articulated consonants and Affricates are both sub-types. If you consider Co-articulated consonants to not count as valid independent morphemes (which as I have explained, is fundamentally wrong), then you should also consider Affricates as non-valid clusters. 

And I really don't understand what your point is. The entire reason why secondary articulations are marked differently in the IPA is to prevent the confusion of having to memorise hundreds or even thousands of ligatures and represented phonemes, it does not mean they do not count. /ʔʷ/ counts as a phoneme in Adyghe because it is an independent sound that contrasts with /ʔ/. Just because it adds an additional '-у' in writing to distinguish the sound does not mean that is a cluster, and a digraph is often used to represent sounds which have no clean single-letter equivalent in orthography. Nobody is arguing that /t͡ʃ/ is not a valid phoneme in English because it is a digraph, 'ch' most of the time. If you seriously need examples of where Adyghe contrasts the plain and labialised glottal stop, here you go.

/ʔa/ (Ӏа) meaning 'hand/arm'
/ʔʷa/ (Ӏуа) meaning 'to say/to speak'
/ʔə/ (Ӏэ) meaning 'to hold'
/ʔʷə/ (Ӏуэ) meaning 'mouth/to graze'

and these are just two minimal pairs of a plain glottal stop versus a glottal stop with simultaneous rounding of the lips. That is quite literally the only difference, and as such they are separate phonemes.

I do not understand where you get the idea that proto-circassian had 170 consonants. You are assuming that every single consonant, or the majority of consonants, has multiple secondary articulations, which is simply incorrect. Again, for the last time, the only reason why secondary articulations are superscript is because it would take too much effort and complexity trying to make a palatalised, uvularised, pharyngealised, labialised, etc. Consonant without having too much to memorise to be feasible. It is infinitely easier to just add small little superscript letters after the base letter to create new sounds in notation. Most linguists reconstruct Proto-Circassian as having 50~60 consonants (INCLUDING secondary articulations) with 2 to 3 vowels. So not 170 or 'thousands' like you are suggesting. No idea where you got that answer from, even in the most maximalising count in language like ǃXóõ, it does not even have over 200 phonemes. 

And in the example which you are trying to prove to me that English has labialised consonants, as you decide to analyse 'quick' as /kʷɪkʰ/, you are using flawed methodology. Since the first 'k' is not aspirated as it is a cluster, which boils down to the basics of English pronunciation, it cannot be conceived that /kʷ/ is a phoneme. If it were aspirated /kʰʷ/, then yes, it would be a phoneme, but since it isn't, it cannot be counted as a phoneme, as all voiceless consonants in English are aspirated outside of clusters; it is a very basic concept.

Old English was designed to be written in Runes, but if we tried to write modern English in Runes, it would simply not work. Too many vowel sounds, too many different consonants, and overall it would be too much of a hassle. Although I dislike the current English orthography in its phonetic reflection, it tells us so much about the history of the language, and replacing it would take away the mutual intelligibility in writing which English speakers enjoy today. And English isn't even that inconsistent when we reverse the great vowel shift. You can write in your own English orthography in your own time, but the current is honestly fine.

Proto-Germanic actually lost its labialised phonemes. PIE /hʷ/ became PG /hʷ/, which later merged into /w/ in the vast majority of English dialects, yours likely included. Next, PIE /gʷ/ became voiceless /kʷ/ in PG, which later shifted to /h/, like in Horse. Though it is retained in some English words like 'queen', it is analysed as a cluster, or /kw/, not an independent morpheme, for reasons I have already listed. Lastly, PIE /gʷʰ/, like in /gʷʰéntis/, shifted to /g/ in PG, or /gundiz/ as it is reconstructed. Even in the case of /kw/, no native English speaker realises it as an independent morpheme /kʷ/. Go ahead, ask other English people, none of them will agree with you. And for the case of English, no dialect (asides from those which replace /t, d/ with /ɾ/, which isn't a contrasting phoneme for numerous reasons) has more than one fully phonemic rhotic. You bring up the cases of 'wr' sequences, but you will notice that the only difference between 'rap' and 'wrap' is the orthography. No modern English speaker contrasts these, and Even in dialects (or languages) like Doric Scots, the 'wr' sequence has shifted to a 'vr' sequence. All modern English speakers who don't exhibit this shift will pronounce both as homophones. No English speaker contrasts consonants with palatalisation or labialisation, because they are strictly allophonic. Compare this with Adyghe where labialisation is a literal feature of the language, not allophonic variation. I only used the example of 'kick' versus 'quick' to prove that English lacks a distinct /kʷ/ phoneme. Anything that resembles this is a /kw/ cluster.

Also, 'million' (IPA: /mɪl.jən/) does not form a palatal lateral approximant /ʎ/. There is quite literally a syllable boundary, and in words where /l/ and /j/ are in the same syllable (like in 'lute') most modern speakers simply drop the /j/ into a single /l/ phoneme. I know it is fun to think that English could have tons more consonants, but come on, this is just wishful thinking. And I don't know where you got the idea that 'the secondary 'l' in this cluster completely changes the consonant to a lateral fricative'. No English dialect has /ɬ/ as a contrasting phoneme, except ALLOPHONICALLY in clusters, like 'pl', 'kl', 'sl', or 'fl', and even then, this is literally allophonic, meaning that it does not form a minimal pair with regular /l/, for example.

And for the very last time, Proto-Circassian has never been reconstructed with thousands of consonants after applying secondary articulations. The most generous reconstructions, as I have already stated, are only around 60 consonants at most.

And stop calling it 'Kirkassian'. It is 'Circassian', the correct spelling.

replies.author: @Terror_Official
replies.text:
@Ariale618 Secondary articulation is what secondary articulation is, not a secondary consonant sound. There are 3 basic separations of what classify as Consonants. Those are Pulmonic, Non-Pulmonic and Affricates. The ONLY distinction is where the sound is made: using the lungs (Pulmonic), without the lungs (Non-Pulmonic, clicks, ejectives etc), or two separate sounds said in sequence (Affricates, Дж [d͡ʒ] for example as English "j"). The technical fourth, Co-articulated consonants, I separated as digraphs, ligatures, diphthongs, triphthongs and complex graphemes, are what you are arguing (and even then, only half of the classification) as complete consonants even in a cluster.

Your example here of lumping ejectives in with Palatalization is also flawed, as they're fundamentally different sounds (Pulmonic vs Non-Pulmonic) and are given their own IPA just for them; which is why I include them as separate consonants (because they are). When separated from the nearby letter, the ejectives' mark cannot be its own sound the way Ādəɣa articulations can.

For instance in бгъуитӏуӏу [bʁʷi.tʷʼəʔʷ], б-гъу-и.-тӏу-ӏу is the separation. Here ӏ is both used for a glottal stop [ʔ] but also the factor that decides to change т into an ejective [tʼ]. In Georgian for instance, you cannot remove the ejective from Tʼâri and have it go to produce a different sound elsewhere. The phoneme of ტ [t̪ʼ] is one contained consonant because the alphabet is designed for it, but the base consonant below it is always [tʼ], not [t͜ʔ]. This example also shows rounding of an obstructed sound which also would not modify the consonant it's attached to, as glottal stops have no phonation. It may be a consonant, but [ʔʷ] is not a phoneme. It is however a digraph, and a diphthong if you argue it should become [tʼ].

Proto-Kirkassian from my example, if we included all of their base 2nd articulations, would be around 170 consonants. The IPA will not add 170 symbols for every variation of pharyngealization, uvularization, palatalization, labialization, bilabialization, velarization, labio-palatalization, aspiration etc etc, within Proto-Kirkassian or other languages, or modern Ādəɣa just because you believe that [p] and [pʲ] are two different base consonants to you. This is why they have modifier unicode to add these. My point of the word "worse" was not that they make the language worse (I enjoy the complexity, Irish has this same comparison), but that if you want to try counting every example variant combination of [q(ˤ)(ʲ)(ʷ)(ʰ)(ʼ)] as its own consonant (which IPA does not, again) for every consonant in P-C you will be up into the thousands of consonants; where your point is blown out of proportion.

In your example of kick and quick, I'd argue that the first should be spelled as kʰyk and the second as kw̥yk as I do not aspirate the 2nd word nor do I voice it ([w] here is also a co-articulated consonant). English is also a heavily flawed writing system, much to the same as Ādəɣa having to use a foreign system not designed for it. English was designed for writing in Runes and Ādəɣa did not have one accustomed to it like Czech, Greek, Georgian or Armenian.

You give examples of words like quick, but their roots in Proto-Germanic would've been said with these labialized [k]'s using modifier [w]'s that were never elided: kwikwaz [ˈkʷi.kʷɑz] which I'd write as Kʷíkʷâz. The only thing elided in this example is the final suffix, common in P-G shifts. English learned to say Kw differently than it was used before once shifting to Latin alphabet, and then again with standardization of a base alphabet. Each phoneme now has many allophones.

Ādəɣa for instance has two Rhotics, with one modified: Р for [r], Гъ for [ʁ] and a modified Гъу for [ʁʷ].
However, English contains the following Rhotics: [ʁ] [ʀ] [r] [ɾ] [ɻ] [ɹ] [ɹ̠]
Each of these consonants have their own character in IPA because they are all individual Pulmonics. In each example of these rhotics, English typically rounds them for words like wrought, wrath, wren, wrangle, wreathe, wraith and wrap; usually as [ɹʷ].

Attempt to say these words without your lips touching and you'll still be saying the consonant [ɹ], but in what English speakers would consider an odd or particularly Australian way; especially saying wraith as [ɹ̠aɪθ] instead of [ɹʷɛɪθ]. However, you can use any number of palatalization, labialization etc on these rhotics and they do not produce "new" consonants in English.

Your example of [k͜w] being a phoneme is not my opinion, in your instance it's a digraph -- two letters making two sounds, and I did not include it in my list of pʰǭnē̂́mătă.

An example in English of a similar contrast you're for some reason looking for is catnip and million.
Catnip [ˈkætⁿnɪp] preps the [t] phoneme for a subsequent nasal release, but it does not change the consonant of [t] into [tⁿ] in English. However, you speak a word like million [ˈmɪʎ(ə~ɪ)n], and the secondary l in this cluster completely changes the consonant to a lateral fricative (a new consonant to my list).

Here tn is a combination forming a modified [tⁿ] consonant, while ll is forming a ligature-like diphthong, changing from [l.l] into [ʎ]. English has this with words like gibbering that bilabialize [ˈd͡ʒɪᵝ.bɚ.ɹɪŋ] before the subsequent [b] depending on your native articulation. It is rare and no English speaker would argue this counts as a new consonant, as most preform a glottal stop instead [ˈd͡ʒɪʔ.bɚ.ɹɪŋ].

Again though, you seem to be caught up on the "worse" in my comment, but it had nothing to do with your language. It had everything to do with what it'd take to count thousands of consonants based on variants of Proto-Kirkassian secondary articulation, not modern Ādəɣa.

replies.author: @Ariale618
replies.text:
@Terror_OfficialYou don't understand what 'secondary articulation' is then. It isn't a 'modifier' of a consonant, but languages with them actually distinguish between them. So the difference between a plain consonant, a labialised consonant, and a palatalised consonant means that they form these funny things called minimal pairs, where two words sound exactly the same but feature different phonemes. Depending on the dialect, there are 50 to 60 consonants in Adyghe, and 47 or 48 in Kabardian (based on whether you count /h/ as a phoneme), and that is if you consider them separate languages. The labialised and ejective 'versions' are fully phonemic sounds as they distinguish words. Do not confuse independent sounds of the same base place of articulation and different secondary manner to clusters.

Let's take an example in English. You might think that 'kick' (ipa: /kʰɪkʰ/) forms a minimal pair with 'quick' (ipa:  /kwɪkʰ/), or even that it is labialised /kʷɪkʰ/. The reason why we can't just consider /kʷ/ as an independent phoneme is because it is realised as a cluster, 'kw'.

So, why can labialised, palatalised, and ejective consonants be considered as independent phonemes in Adyghe but not english? Well it all comes down to the tolerance of clusters. English loves clusters whereas Adyghe often rejects them at its most basic phonological core. 'kw' can't be considered as 'just a cluster' in Adyghe because the language simply doesn't allow clusters in most positions. What might look like a cluster is almost certainly a more recent sound shift where the unstressed schwa vowel /ə/ elided and left a cluster. If you asked an English person to write down the sounds of English, they could take a million years and would never write down 'kw'. If you asked a Circassian, it might be the first sound they write down.

Note that the only reason why Adyghe might seem like it lacks these sounds is because of allophony. Vowels will shift when they are preceded by a labialised, palatalised, uvular, or most types of consonants really. This can give the impression that they don't exist, whereas in reality these same vowels which you might think are phonemes can only occur when they come after the consonant.

Obviously 'kw' is just one example. But considering it a 'phoneme' in English just because you want it to be is not very helpful. If you truly believe that English also has labialised phonemes contrasting with plain phonemes, then give me examples of the 'phoneme' contrasting with the cluster. Adyghe has plenty of words which contrast /qʷ/ (the phoneme) and /qw/ (the cluster). I say this because Adyghe lacks a plain /k/ in native words. And obviously English does not have this contrast. I can give you examples if you truly need me to to convince you that labialisation is an actual feature of a language and not something that makes it 'worse'.

replies.text: @Terror_Official”modified” consonants are absolutely treated as individual sounds in languages that have them, which is very unlike what English does. A sound not being written as a single distinct in it in the IPA has no bearing at all on whether a language treads it as a distinct meaningful sound

replies.text:
Kirkassian have 34 base consonants, 9 diphthongs, 2 modifier characters, 2 vowels (though [a] can be long [aː] as a "3rd"), 5 glide vowels (mainly used for outside languages) and 2 semivowels.

If you don't include Ejectives (which I do because they're separate IPA sounds), they only have 6 diphthongs and 29 consonants. Many of their consonants can also be labialized with [ʷ], though they once pharyngealized [ˤ], labialized [ʷ], palatalized [ʲ] and aspirated [ʰ] most consonants with tons of combinations (even Ejectives), so it once was worse.

If you include the labialized versions (which I don't as they only constitute changes in sound structure if they're vowels), then they have 10 diphthongs and 45 "consonants".

For a nearby example, under the same rules, Georgian has as follows: 15 Vowels, 2 Semivowels, 2 Glide Vowels, 37 base consonants, 2 loaned consonants, 5 diphthongs and 5 modifiers (Palatalization, Aspiration, Nasalization, Velarization and Bilabialization). If you add in its modifiers, then it adds on 4 additional consonants for 41 total, and if you include the long variant of [o] as [oː], then they also had 16 vowels.

A lot of this idea of them having so many consonants is really just articulation of the same base sound. You'd be surprised how many English has by comparison (it's a lot higher than people realize).
